pr_title: posix: add support for mmap, memlock, shared memory, and mprotect
pr_body:
* add support for `_POSIX_MAPPED_FILES`
* add support for `_POSIX_MEMLOCK_RANGE`
* add support for `_POSIX_MEMLOCK` (currently unimplemented / fails with `ENOSYS`)
* add support for `_POSIX_SHARED_MEMORY_OBJECTS`
* add support for `_POSIX_MEMORY_PROTECTION` (currently unimplemented / fails with `ENOSYS`)

**Shared Memory Objects and Memory-Mapped Files**

On systems that support mapping anonymous memory (i.e. have an MMU and lots of RAM), shared memory objects are implemented using `k_mem_map()` and friends (i.e. a shared memory object is comprised of a number of blocks of virtual memory that are `CONFIG_MMU_PAGE_SIZE` in size). On systems that do not have an MMU, shared memory objects are implemented with heap allocation.

Note: it is up to the particular vtable implementor, to support the `ZFD_IOCTL_MMAP` operation. However, there would still need to be some integration with `msync()` in order to synchronize writes to e.g. a regular file. From that perspective, shared memory objects were an easy prototyping option.

A potential future improvement on shared memory objects would be to support a separate `ioctl()` to attach statically allocated memory.

**z_finalize_typed_fd()**

A particular change to highlight in this case though, is adding a `mode` field to `struct fd_entry`, which allows fdtable code to identify which subsystem or API a file descriptor belongs to, and to react accordingly. The `z_finalize_typed_fd()` function allows us to differentiate between fifo, char device, message queue, directory, semaphore, block device, shared memory, regular file, symbolic link, and socket.

In fact, the same 32-bit `mode` field _should_ also have the file access mode tied to it, rather than the physical file (which is currently the case now for the FS subsystem, and should be considered a bug). It's trivial to consider a case where one file descriptor is used for writing to a file and another file descriptor is used for reading from a file. Both file descriptors point to the same physical file, but each has different access modes and offsets (addressed below).

**Per-file Offsets**

Another similar adjustment to `struct fd_entry` is to have a per-fd (per `FILE*`) offset, which is just consistent with the C/C++, POSIX (all?) programming models of "files".

A few drive-by fixes aside from that, shuffling things between zvfs, posix, and fs, as-needed.

[Doc Preview](https://builds.zephyrproject.io/zephyr/pr/73799/docs/services/portability/posix/index.html)

Fixes #59950
Fixes #59951
Fixes #59952
Fixes #59953
pr_comments: Some platforms seem to have `CONFIG_MMU` but do not implement `arch_mem_map()` or `arch_mem_unmap()`, so there may be a couple of exclusions in `tests/posix/shm/testcase.yaml`

Here's the worst offenders I've encountered.

In `munmap()` you shouldn't call `arch_page_phys_get()` as this will
return -EFAULT if the first page is paged out. Should call `k_mem_unmap()`
directly.

Side note: I think `k_mem_unmap()` should return an error code instead of
void. May always be 0 for now but the prototype should be ready.

`shm_mmap()` looks interesting. This:

- `arch_page_phys_get(shm->mem, &phys)`

followed by:

- `*virt = k_mem_phys_map(phys + off, ROUND_UP(len, _page_size), K_MEM_PERM_RW)`

is going to produce very surprizing results with demand paging indeed.
First, because you use `k_mem_phys_map()` you are bypassing the very tiny
protection against having a physical page mapped twice. It is kinda OK only
with pinned memory which is another way to say that demand paging doesn't
support it.

In your case, what would happen is that you get a second mapping at a 
different virtual address but one that is not tracked by the physical page 
frame management code. So if memory pressure increases and `shm->mem` is not
accessed _irrespective_ of how often that second virtual mapping is used then
the `shm->mem` virtual address will be a prime candidate to be paged out.
And when that happens, the underlying physical page will be recycled for
some other content accessible through some other virtual address that now
will also be visible through the mapping you created with that
`k_mem_phys_map()`, and such content no longer having anything to do with 
the initial `shm->mem` content. And yet, if `shm->mem` is accessed again,
it is unlikely that its content will be paged back into the same physical
page.

In short, this is no good!  ;-)

Now... why do you need a second mapping? Zephyr uses a flat address space
model shared by all threads. Just return `shm->mem` from shm_mmap()`, turn
`shm_unmmap()` into a no-op and be done with it.

Eventually it would make sense to leverage memory domains if this is going
to be used in user space so that a shared memory block is part of the same 
memory protection domain.

- [x] remove unneeded headers from `mlock.c` (requested by @ycsin)
- [x] add a compatible `MAP_ANONYMOUS` to force an anonymous mapping in `mmap.c` (requested by @andyross)
- [ ] attempted to call `k_mem_unmap()` directly in `mmap.c`, but that triggers an assert in `mmu.c`, so kept it for now
- [x] use `shm->mem` for all file descriptors and 1 virtual mapping shared among file descriptors (request by @npitre)

> you found why you are calling unmap twice 

I am calling unmap twice because you said I should not check first to see if the region is mapped. Previously I had a call to see if the region was mapped.

Aside from that, it would duplicate a lot of effort to keep track of all mapped pages in a second location not really part of the kernel or arch.

> it is not
> OK to use it to dodge the assertion on a double unmap.

But it is ok to for any random bit of code to crash the system by calling k_mem_unmap() with a garbage argument? That seems like an obvious gap in testing.

It's not the user's responsibility to manage system resources, it's the kernel's responsibility.

Another issue is that your change will make the function to bail out in the middle of the for loop, leaving already mapped memory after the failing one possibly forever mapped, and never released. A more appropriate place to bail would be where the guard pages are checked. Moreover, the callers actually have to make sure they are unmapping with the same parameters when the region is mapped.

For you to actually hit that assert, you have to pass the two checks for the guard pages first. That means something is horribly wrong for a page in middle of that region to be unmapped. Another reason might be that you are unmapping across multiple virtual regions at the same time. So the boundary guard pages checks would pass, but when you are looping through the pages, you encounter the guard pages in between. For example, region A and region B with guard pages G: `GAAAGGBBBG`. You trying to unmap the whole thing which means the assert would be raised on the middle `GG` guard pages.

Also, this is a very low level API, not to mention being a kernel internal one, one must exercise extreme caution when using it (and also the corresponding mapping function). If garbage arguments are passed to these functions, it is either a coding error, or that memory has been corrupted (e.g. stack overflow, or incorrect pointer de-reference, or cosmic rays). So bailing would be a wise choice in the later case, as correct operations of the whole system can no longer be guaranteed.

I realize that it is low level / not extremely frequently used code, etc, so I knew that there would be rough edges. This is why I've marked mmap as experimental.

I'll revert back to check first using the `arch_` function, since there seems to be no way to otherwise unmap memory using the POSIX model without crashing the system (the POSIX model being that pages can be mapped to more than one virtual memory address, and the kernel doesn't panic when it's told to unmap an invalid address).

> It's not the user's responsibility to manage system resources, it's the
> kernel's responsibility.

Sorry, but the POSIX layer you're creating (and that's highly appreciated
by the way) is _not_ user code. You are managing many different resources
already on behalf of code calling the POSIX interface. That code is the user
not the interface.

Knowing how many times a particular object has been mapped and unmapped is 
the POSIX layer's responsibility, just like the refcounting you already do
elsewhere between `malloc()` and `free()`. You wouldn't free the same memory
twice, right? And you're not calling into the low-level heap allocator to test
if a particular address is still allocated before calling `free()` either.
The assertion in `k_mem_unmap()` is there to catch the equivalent of a
double-free, which is a bug and why it shouldn't be removed.

So it should be no different with `k_mem_map()` and `k_mem_unmap()`.
The first caller to increment the refcount does the map, subsequent callers 
only increment the refcount and get the same already mapped address, and the
last to decrement the count to 0 does the unmap.

@nashif - I think a `k_` prefix is fine for things like `z_finalize_fd()`, etc, but for consistency, that should likely just be a wrapper around a `zvfs_` prefixed function (mutual dependency library of net, fs, posix, libc, etc, where common socket / fs / fd stuff was heading since 2022, #51211). There will be a fair number of `zvfs_` prefixed functions, so I wouldn't necessarily want to flood the `k_` namespace with them.

> I think a `k_` prefix is fine for things like `z_finalize_fd()`

`k_` should be reserved for kernel/ stuff only, let not mix things up.

> Am I missing something that would prevents such implementation?

Of course I am. `munmap()` doesn't pass a fd or any identifier other than
the actual address and length.

But you have another problem here. `k_mem_map_phys_bare()` should be paired
only with `k_mem_unmap_phys_bare()` otherwise bad things will happen.
I'd suggest you use `k_mem_map_phys_guard()` here instead, as it is
much closer to be compatible with `k_mem_unmap()` aka
`k_mem_unmap_phys_guard()`.

And yet `k_mem_unmap_phys_guard()` wants to know if this is about anonymous
mem or not which can probably be determined programmatically (whether there
is a corresponding page frame or backing store entry for it) but that is not
implemented now.

So to say that `MAP_FIXED` is not implementable at the moment due to those
details and it might make sense to simply return `ENOTSUP` for the time being.

issue_context.title: posix: implement `shm_unlink()`
issue_context.body:
There are currently 20 missing POSIX functions with trivial implementations, `shm_unlink()` is one of them.

> shm_unlink - remove a shared memory object (REALTIME)
> 
> The shm_unlink() function shall remove the name of the shared memory object named by the string pointed to by name.
> 
> If one or more references to the shared memory object exist when the object is unlinked, the name shall be removed before shm_unlink() returns, but the removal of the memory object contents shall be postponed until all open and map references to the shared memory object have been removed.
> 
> Even if the object continues to exist after the last shm_unlink(), reuse of the name shall subsequently cause [shm_open()](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/shm_open.html) to behave as if no shared memory object of this name exists (that is, [shm_open()](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/shm_open.html) will fail if O_CREAT is not set, or will create a new shared memory object if O_CREAT is set).

See https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/shm_unlink.html

See RFC #51211 for more info.

Driving by, haven't had time for a full review but this all looks pretty straightforward:

Is MAP_ANON/MAP_ANONYMOUS not part of POSIX?  You probably want that here for portability, since that's the primary mechanism in linux.  Linux will ignore the fd argument if it's set (it doesn't have to be -1).  This code will use the fd only, meaning that Linux code that gets ported to it (i.e. drops the MAP_ANONYMOUS flag) and forgets to pass -1 in the fd argument (because it was never needed) is going to misbehave.

Currently, it doesn't seem that there is a generic API to flush anonymously mapped pages. Also from what I understand, the memories used in this implementation so far use synchronized writes. I could double-check that though.

Eventually, when mapping regular files is implemented by the fs subsystem, there will need to be an ISR to catch writes, and those might also be buffered, but that's a future problem.

Otherwise, it may be useful to integrate the cache API eventually, but it's probably also premature at this point.

https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/hardware/cache/index.html

Yeah, actually, so `k_mem_map_impl()` does not support explicit caching flags, so all writes will be synchronous. There is no need to fail, since doing nothing still has the expected result.

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/453ab8a9a356acf475a965a777a370795effa255/kernel/mmu.c#L581

I have a little concern about the unions here resulting in some difficult to find bugs for future implementers. I guess the other option would be to have these separate, but that would take additional space, but is that a lot?

Pushing an extra, unused, argument onto the stack and popping it back off shouldn't be too much of a concern I would think. But up to 16 extra (unneeded / unused) bytes per file descriptor might be a lot of wasted space, especially given that most seekable file types should eventually adopt the `_offset()` variants, and the two functions are otherwise identical.

It should be noted as well, that offsets do not apply to sockets, pipes, etc, just regular files and memory, and right now regular files don't even support per-fd offsets, just memory 😅 

That's technically a bug, as well, so can be fixed post feature freeze.
I guess I was more concerned with the subtle semantic difference. If the implementation is an offset, but the caller is expecting without, that offset argument will be read as garbage.

Interestingly, `lseek()` must be able to set the file descriptor offset to an arbitrary value. Kind of mind boggling.

> The lseek() function shall allow the file offset to be set beyond the end of the existing data in the file.

https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/lseek.html

Consequently, read and write implementations must be able to decide if an offset is valid or invalid and react accordingly.

So they should be able to handle garbage.

Interestingly, `lseek()` must be able to set the file descriptor offset to an arbitrary value. Kind of mind boggling.

> The lseek() function shall allow the file offset to be set beyond the end of the existing data in the file.

https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/lseek.html

Consequently, read and write implementations must be able to decide if an offset is valid or invalid and react accordingly.

So they should be able to handle garbage.
